                      fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4, fig.retina = 2)

# Why dependent variables need a correction

The false discovery rate (FDR) guarantee of the T-Rex selector rests on the exchangeability of the null
variables and the dummies along the solution path. Independent dummies are exchangeable with independent
null variables. When the variables are strongly dependent, a null variable that is correlated with an
active one enters the path earlier than an independent dummy would, so the dummies no longer mirror the
nulls and the false discovery proportion (FDP) estimate becomes anti-conservative. The dependency-aware
T-Rex selector (T-Rex+DA) [@machkour2025datrex] restores the control by estimating the dependency
structure and by deflating the vote within groups of dependent variables. It has been applied to sparse
index tracking with autoregressive and nearest-neighbour stock dependency models
[@machkour2025indextracking; @machkour2024ar1].

# An autoregressive design

The variables follow a first-order autoregressive (AR(1)) process across the columns with coefficient
0.7, and five of them are active.

```{r data}
set.seed(321)
n <- 100
p <- 100
rho <- 0.7
X <- matrix(0, n, p)
X[, 1] <- rnorm(n)
for (j in 2:p) X[, j] <- rho * X[, j - 1] + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(n)
true_support <- c(10, 30, 50, 70, 90)
beta <- numeric(p)
beta[true_support] <- 2
y <- as.numeric(X %*% beta + rnorm(n))
```

The plain selector and the dependency-aware selector on the same data and the same seed.

```{r compare}
plain <- TRexSelector$new(X, y, tFDR = 0.1, seed = 7, verbose = FALSE,
                          control = trex_control(K = 10))
plain$select()
da <- TRexDASelector$new(X, y, tFDR = 0.1, seed = 7, verbose = FALSE,
                         da_control = trex_da_control(da_method = "BT"),
                         control = trex_control(K = 10))
da$select()
data.frame(selector = c("T-Rex", "T-Rex+DA"),
           selected = c(length(plain$selected_indices), length(da$selected_indices)),
           FDP = c(trex_fdp(plain$selected_indices, true_support),
                   trex_fdp(da$selected_indices, true_support)),
           TPP = c(trex_tpp(plain$selected_indices, true_support),
                   trex_tpp(da$selected_indices, true_support)))
```

`TRexDASelector` inherits the fields of `TRexSelector` (`selected_indices`, `fdp_hat_mat`, `T_stop`,
`L`, ...) and adds the record of the dependency estimation.

```{r fields}
da$da_method_used
da$rho_thresh
round(da$rho_grid, 3)
```

# The dependency methods

`trex_da_control(da_method = )` chooses how the dependency is handled.

| Method | Dependency model | Parameters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"BT"` (default) | binary tree: hierarchical clustering of the variables at correlation thresholds, the threshold is calibrated on a grid | `hc_linkage`, `hc_grid_length` |
| `"NN"` | nearest neighbours: a correlation-threshold sweep of the same form | `hc_grid_length` |
| `"AR1"` | first-order autoregressive: a variable is compared with its neighbours inside a window | `cor_coef` (estimated when `-2`), `rho_thr_DA` |
| `"EQUI"` | equi-correlated: a variable is compared with all other variables | `cor_coef` (estimated when `-2`), `rho_thr_DA` |

Each method stands for the dependency model of its paper and is made for data that follow that model. The
binary tree method follows the hierarchical graphical model of [@machkour2025datrex]. It is made for
variables that form disjoint groups of highly correlated variables, and it was studied with one active
variable per group. The autoregressive method follows [@machkour2024ar1]. It is made for variables whose
correlation decays with their distance in the column order, as in a first-order autoregressive process,
and it does not assume one active variable per group. The nearest-neighbour method follows
[@machkour2025indextracking]. It is made for overlapping groups of highly correlated variables, as they
are characteristic for stock returns. The equi-correlated method is made for variables that all share one
correlation.

The binary tree method clusters the variables by correlation distance with the linkage `hc_linkage`
(single by default), evaluates the FDP estimate at `hc_grid_length` correlation thresholds (the default
`0` lets the core take $\min(20, p)$ points) and keeps the threshold `rho_thresh`.

The binary tree method, the nearest-neighbour method and the prior groups evaluate every step on the
whole grid of correlation thresholds. The L-loop and the T-loop read the FDP estimate at one of them,
the reference threshold, which sits at three quarters of the grid (element 15 of the default 20). The
selection then searches all cells of stopping time, voting level and threshold, and `rho_thresh` is the
threshold of the cell it takes. The inherited fields `fdp_hat_mat`, `phi_mat` and `phi_prime` therefore
hold the values at the reference threshold, while `r_mat`, `v_thresh` and the selection belong to
`rho_thresh`. The values at every threshold are in `FDP_hat_array_BT`, `Phi_array_BT` and `R_array_BT`.

The autoregressive and equi-correlated methods draw the same independent dummies as the other methods
and penalize the relative occurrences. The autoregressive method compares a variable with the neighbours
inside a window that reaches `ceiling(log(rho_thr_DA) / log(abs(cor_coef)))` columns to each side, up to
the first lag whose correlation `abs(cor_coef)^lag` has fallen to `rho_thr_DA`, a threshold in $[0, 1)$.
The equi-correlated method compares a variable with all other variables and is skipped when
`abs(cor_coef)` does not exceed `rho_thr_DA`. Both methods use the magnitude of the coefficient. Setting
`cor_coef` to `-2` estimates the coefficient from the data, and any other value outside $[-1, 1]$ gives
a warning and is replaced by the estimate.

```{r ar1}
ar1 <- TRexDASelector$new(X, y, tFDR = 0.1, seed = 7, verbose = FALSE,
                          da_control = trex_da_control(da_method = "AR1"),
                          control = trex_control(K = 10))
ar1$select()
ar1$selected_indices
round(ar1$cor_coef, 3)
```

# The penalty of the last step

All five methods penalize the relative occurrences in the same way. With $\Phi_t(j)$ the relative
occurrence of variable $j$ after $t$ included dummies (step $t$ of the T-loop) and $T$ the stopping time
at which the path is evaluated, its last step, the selector works with

$$
\Phi_t^{\mathrm{DA}}(j) = \Psi_T(j) \, \Phi_t(j), \qquad
\Psi_T(j) = \frac{1}{2 - \min_{j'} |\Phi_T(j) - \Phi_T(j')|}, \qquad t = 1, \dots, T,
$$

where $j'$ runs over the variables that $j$ is compared with, its group, its window or all other
variables. A variable without a group gets $\Psi_T(j) = 1/2$.

This is a deliberate deviation from the papers. Read literally, they recompute the penalty at every step,
$\Psi_t(j)$ from $\Phi_t$, while the selector takes the penalty of the last step for all steps. The
reason is the FDP estimator. It sums over the increments
$\Phi_t^{\mathrm{DA}}(j) - \Phi_{t-1}^{\mathrm{DA}}(j)$ and counts expected false discoveries only while
no increment is negative. One penalty per variable keeps the increments non-negative. A penalty per step
does not, because the penalty of a variable changes from step to step, and the FDP estimate then becomes
too small.

A Monte Carlo comparison of the two constructions with 1,000 runs per setting on block, autoregressive
and independent designs supports the choice. With the nearest-neighbour method the per-step penalty
exceeded a target FDR of 0.1, with 0.15 on an independent design and 0.13 on a block design, where the
last-step penalty gave 0.00 and 0.03. No setting had the last-step penalty above the target and the
per-step penalty below it. The per-step penalty selected more variables only where its estimate was
invalid, and on autoregressive designs the last-step penalty had the higher true positive rate. The
methods `"AR1"` and `"EQUI"` used the per-step penalty up to TRexSelector 2.0.1, so their selections can
differ slightly from earlier versions, while `"BT"`, `"NN"` and the prior groups have always used the
penalty of the last step.

# Prior groups

When the groups of dependent variables are known, pass them as `prior_groups`, a list of integer
vectors of length $p$ with a group label per variable. The dependency estimation then runs within the
given groups: hierarchical clustering inside each group, and the calibration grid is built from the
within-group dendrogram heights. The deflation acts on data-driven neighbourhoods inside the known
groups, never on the raw groups themselves. Several levels can be supplied, and their finest common
refinement is the constraint.

```{r prior}
blocks <- rep(1:10, each = 10)
pg <- TRexDASelector$new(X, y, tFDR = 0.1, seed = 7, verbose = FALSE,
                         da_control = trex_da_control(prior_groups = list(blocks)),
                         control = trex_control(K = 10))
pg$select()
pg$selected_indices
```

# Greedy solvers under T-Rex+DA

The deflation relies on the spread of occurrences within a group of dependent variables. A greedy
solver (`"TOMP"`, `"TOOLS"`, `"TGP"`, `"TACGP"`, `"TMP"`, `"TNCGMP"` and `"TAFS"`) picks the top
candidate of a tie deterministically and removes that spread. The exchangeable-tie band restores it,
since statistically indistinguishable top candidates within a correlated cluster are then picked
uniformly at random per step. T-Rex+DA therefore runs a greedy solver with a band of 0.25 unless the
control sets it. `exch_tie_alpha` in `trex_control()` takes another width, and 0 switches the band off.
The path solvers ignore the option.

Without the band the greedy solvers can exceed the target FDR at a high correlation. In a Monte Carlo
study on AR(1) designs with a correlation of 0.9 (1,000 runs per setting, target FDR 0.2) each of the
seven greedy solvers had an FDR of 0.21 to 0.27 without the band and of 0.13 to 0.17 with it, at a
true positive rate lower by 0.07 to 0.13. At correlations up to 0.8 the target held without the band
as well, and the band cost 0.03 to 0.05 of the true positive rate there.

```{r greedy}
greedy <- TRexDASelector$new(X, y, tFDR = 0.1, seed = 7, verbose = FALSE,
                             da_control = trex_da_control(da_method = "BT"),
                             control = trex_control(solver = "TOMP", K = 10))
greedy$select()
greedy$selected_indices
```

# Examples

The [TRexSelector_Examples](https://github.com/trexselector/TRexSelector_Examples/tree/main)
repository holds runnable demos and Monte Carlo studies of T-Rex+DA under autoregressive, block,
heavy-tailed, grouped, nearest-neighbour and equi-correlated dependency, with their results and a
README per demo, in
[R](https://github.com/trexselector/TRexSelector_Examples/tree/main/R/trex_selector_methods/ad/trex_da),
[Python](https://github.com/trexselector/TRexSelector_Examples/tree/main/Python/trex_selector_methods/ad/trex_da)
and
[C++](https://github.com/trexselector/TRexSelector_Examples/tree/main/cpp/trex_selector_methods/ad/trex_da).

```{r teardown, include = FALSE}
trex_set_num_threads(old_threads)
```
